title: Progressive ataxia and palatal tremor (PAPT) with hypertrophic olivary degeneration (HOD): A case report
case_prompt: A 57-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of synchronous rhythmic movements of the soft palate, progressive dysarthria, limb incoordination when reaching for objects, and gait difficulty. He had no relevant medical or family history. On examination, he had a wide-based gait, inability to tandem-walk, exaggerated speech (explosive dysarthria), upper limb dysmetria, gaze-evoked and rebound nystagmus, and a broadened stance. Routine laboratory studies, including thyroid-stimulating hormone, vitamin B12, antinuclear antibodies, lactate, and phytanic acid, were normal. Tests for paraneoplastic ataxia were negative. Audiometry, nerve conduction studies, and EMG were normal. CT of the head was unremarkable, and evoked potentials were within normal limits. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral enlargement of the inferior olivary nuclei with increased signal intensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR images and no evidence of cerebellar atrophy or supratentorial abnormalities.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of acute brainstem or cerebellar lesions such as hemorrhage, infarction, or trauma — “Palatal myoclonus can be also caused by acute lesions such as brainstem or cerebellar hemorrhage, infarction, or trauma. In this case, the clinical context and imaging can eliminate these diagnoses.”  
2. Consideration of demyelinating, neoplastic, or infectious bulbar lesions — “HOD should not be confused with other bulbar lesions such as demyelination, tumor or infection, which also presents a high signal intensity on proton density and T2-weighted images, with possible enhancement after injection of Gadolinium. It may mimics the finding of HOD, whereas HOD never enhances.”  
3. Secondary HOD from a Guillain-Mollaret triangle lesion — “Finally, the hypertrophic olivary degeneration occurring in the context of PAPT syndrome cannot be confused with that which is secondary to a lesion of the Guillain-Mollaret triangle. In the latter case, it is always accompanied by a causal structural lesion, whereas in the PAPT syndrome, it occurs in isolation.”  
4. PAPT as the unifying diagnosis given palatal tremor, progressive cerebellar ataxia, bulbar signs, and isolated HOD on MRI — “The syndrome of progressive ataxia and palatal tremor (PAPT) is a rare, slowly progressive neurodegenerative disorder with palatal tremor, cerebellar ataxia, and bulbar features.”
